summary:
This is the first page of the **detailed contents** (which runs PDF pp.8-16). It covers:

**Front matter** (printed roman numerals as shown in the book; PDF pages in parentheses — the book's printed roman folios are 2 lower than PDF numbering):
- preface xv (p.17)
- acknowledgments xvii (p.19)
- about this book xviii (p.20) — who should read the book, the road map (p.21), and "About the code" (p.22)
- about the authors xxi (p.23)
- about the cover illustration xxii (p.24)

**Chapter 1, What is deep learning?** — printed p. 1 (PDF p.25). Its sections (PDF pages = printed + 24):

- 1.1 Artificial intelligence, machine learning, and deep learning — p.26
- 1.2 Artificial intelligence — p.26
- 1.3 Machine learning — p.27
- 1.4 Learning rules and representations from data — p.28
- 1.5 The “deep” in “deep learning” — p.31
- 1.6 Understanding how deep learning works, in three figures — p.32
- 1.7 What makes deep learning different — p.34
- 1.8 The age of generative AI — p.35
- 1.9 What deep learning has achieved so far — p.35
- 1.10 Beware of the short-term hype — p.36
- 1.11 Summer can turn to winter — p.38
- 1.12 The promise of AI — p.38

**Reading the structure of chapter 1.** It first defines the nested fields — AI, machine learning, deep learning (1.1-1.3) — then explains learning as finding useful **representations** of data (1.4) and what "deep" means: many successive layers of representations (1.5). Section 1.6 explains the mechanism in three figures (layers parameterized by weights, a loss function measuring error, an optimizer adjusting weights). Sections 1.7-1.9 explain why deep learning displaced earlier methods, the arrival of generative AI, and achievements so far. The chapter closes with a caution about hype, the history of "AI winters", and a longer-term optimistic outlook (1.10-1.12).

**How to use it:** the preface and "about this book" are worth reading before chapter 1 — they explain the code-first approach, prerequisites (reasonable Python, high-school math) and how to run the code (Keras on JAX, TensorFlow or PyTorch; Colab).

concepts.name: Learning representations from data
concepts.definition: Automatically finding transformations of input data that make a task (e.g., classification) easier.
concepts.intuition: Rotating your viewpoint until two tangled groups of points become separable by a straight line.
concepts.technical: Each layer of a deep network applies a parameterized transformation; training adjusts parameters so the final representation makes the target easy to predict.
concepts.significance: Section 1.4 frames all of machine learning this way; deep learning stacks many such layers (1.5).
concepts.example: Changing coordinates so that black and white points become separable by x > 0 (a typical illustration).
concepts.misconception: Representations are not hand-designed in deep learning; they are learned.
